title.en: The Mani Walls: Prayers Built into the Landscape

region.en: Mani walls of eastern Tibet, near Kanze (symbolic pin at Kanze, Kham)
region.zh: 康區甘孜一帶的嘛呢牆（以甘孜為象徵定位）

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Land of the Lamas (1891)

summary.en: The Tibetans have another way of showing their religious feelings, that love of mankind dear to Buddhism: this is, in multiplying for the weal of sentient creation written or sculptured copies of the mani prayer. It is no uncommon thing to pass a family established under a tent in a locality where shaly stones are abundant, every member busily occupied incising on slabs of rock the sacred formula, and building up after months, perhaps years, of labor a 'mani wall', each stone in it having the prayer sculptured on it and frequently carefully painted; walls a hundred yards and more long and eight or ten feet high. Others will shape the letters composing the prayer with blocks of white stone on some far-seen mountain side, giving them such huge dimensions that they can be read four or five miles away.
summary.zh: 藏人以另一方式表達宗教情懷——佛教所珍視的「愛眾」之心：為一切有情之福，不斷雕刻、書寫六字真言。常見一家人支帳於頁巖豐富之地，全家日日於石片上刻經；積數月乃至數年之功，壘成「嘛呢牆」——每塊石上皆刻經文且常加彩繪，牆長可逾百步、高八九英尺。更有以白色石塊於遠望可見的山坡上砌出咒字，其大可於四五里外誦讀。

sensitivity.note: Living devotional practice; paraphrase of public-domain travel record.

passages.text: It is no uncommon thing to pass a family established under a tent in a locality where shaly stones are abundant, every member busily occupied incising on slabs of rock the sacred formula, and building up after months, perhaps years, of labor a mani wall, each stone in it having the prayer sculptured on it and frequently carefully painted; I have seen these walls a hundred yards and more long, and eight or ten feet high. Others will shape the letters composing the prayer with blocks of white stone on some far-seen mountain side, giving them such huge dimensions that they can be read four or five miles away.

passages.text: Small stones on which this prayer is sculptured are continually offered to one by beggars, who are paid for them by a handful of tsamba or a little tea; and a person of any respectability never dreams of refusing to buy all offered to him, placing them along the walls of his house, or else on the nearest mani wall.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Land of the Lamas (1891); not verbatim.

title.en: The Hairy Savages of the Northern Desert

region.en: Desert of northern Tibet, on the caravan road (symbolic pin in the Changtang)
region.zh: 藏北高原商路（以羌塘為象徵定位）

texts.period: Tibetan travellers' tales, collected by W. W. Rockhill, 1891

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Land of the Lamas (1891)

summary.en: An old lama from Rewang gomba described most graphically the journey of the caravan he had joined through the desert of northern Tibet, and the attacks made on it by small parties of brigands; several times, he said, his party had met hairy savages, with long, tangled locks falling around them like cloaks, naked, speechless beings, hardly human, who threw stones at the travellers but, having no arms, could do but little harm. This story of hairy savages Rockhill had often heard from Tibetans while at Peking, and was convinced that it has its origin in travellers seeing bears standing erect - in northern Tibet these brutes are numerous and large, and their tracks, especially those of the hind paws, have some resemblance to those made by men with naked feet.
summary.zh: 一位自拉薩返鄉的老喇嘛，繪聲繪色講述其商隊穿越藏北荒漠、屢遭小股強人（果洛）襲擊的經歷；又說途中數遇「毛人」——長髮披散如氅、赤身無言、幾非人類之物，向旅人投石，因無兵器故難以傷人。羅克漢在北京時已屢聞此說，認為其實起於旅人望見直立的熊：藏北熊多而巨，其足印（尤後掌）與赤足人跡極為相似。

sensitivity.note: Folk belief recorded by a 19th-century traveller; treated respectfully as heritage of Tibetan travel-lore. The 'Yeti' identification with bears is Rockhill's own rationalist note, reported as such.

passages.text: An old lama from Rewang gomba, some five days' journey south of Lusar, stopped at my inn on his way home from Lhasa; he described most graphically the journey of the caravan he had joined, through the desert of northern Tibet, and the attacks made on it by small parties of brigands. Several times, he said, his party had met hairy savages, with long, tangled locks falling around them like cloaks, naked, speechless beings, hardly human, who threw stones at the travellers, but who, having no arms, could do but little harm.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Land of the Lamas (1891); not verbatim.

passages.text: This story of hairy savages I had often heard from Tibetans, while at Peking, and I was interested at hearing it again; from many things that happened later, on my journey, I am convinced that this story has its origin in travellers seeing bears standing erect. In northern Tibet these brutes are numerous and large, and people who are in constant dread of meeting brigands take the bears, seen probably at a distance, for them; this notion is further strengthened by the sight of their tracks, which, especially those of the hind paws, have some resemblance to those made by men with naked feet.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Land of the Lamas (1891); not verbatim.

title.en: The Story-Tellers and the Ripa Mummers

region.en: Village squares of eastern Tibet (symbolic pin at Ta-chien-lu)
region.zh: 康區打箭爐等地村落（以打箭爐為象徵定位）

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Land of the Lamas (1891)

summary.en: Besides the very large religious literature extant in Tibet there are a number of works of a semi-biographical nature, called nam-t'ar, histories, and translations of Chinese standard works; also books of songs and a few of pure fiction, these latter of Chinese origin and published probably by Chinese enterprise. The nam-t'ar are the favourite compositions, just as the historical novel is the most popular literature throughout China, and quite a numerous class of men earn their livelihood by giving readings of these books; these story-tellers afford the nearest approach the people have to theatrical representations, if we except the Ripa or itinerant mummers (mostly boys) who with hideous masks over their heads perform a grotesque dance to the music of their song, whose burden was a courting of one's expected generosity, becoming fulsome praise when one gave them anything.
summary.zh: 除浩繁宗教典籍外，藏地尚有半傳記性之「南木特爾」（聖者傳）、史書、漢文譯本、歌集，以及少數純虛構之書（多源於漢地）。南木特爾最為風行，一如歷史演義之於中國；賴此為生之說書人自成一行，於市井誦講——他們是藏人最接近戲劇的存在，若不算那些頭戴猙獰面具、邊歌邊舞的流浪「麗巴」（多為男孩），其歌辭之核心不外乎討賞，得賞則讚不絕口。

sensitivity.note: Living performance tradition; paraphrase of public-domain travel record.

passages.text: There are in this country certain festivals, but of a religious character and performed by the lamas, such as the Chamba ch'u-k'or, or Procession of the god Chamba (Maitreya) around the temples, to drive away demons, the festivities of the Lu-gon gyabo dung-dri, or Expulsion of the Prince of Devils, etc., which present much analogy to the mediaeval mystery plays - but these are not given for the amusement of the people, and form no part of their life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Land of the Lamas (1891); not verbatim.

title.en: The Evening Prayer and the Juniper Smoke

region.en: Villages of the Horba states, eastern Tibet (symbolic pin at Kanze)
region.zh: 康區霍爾巴諸部村落（以甘孜為象徵定位）

source.work: W. W. Rockhill, The Land of the Lamas (1891)

summary.en: The most pleasing ceremony noted among them is the evening prayer, observed by nearly every one in the larger villages and towns: as night falls lamps are lit on the altars of every Buddhist temple, and a short service is chanted, while lamas seated on the porch play a rather mournful hymn on long copper horns and clarinets. This is the signal for the housewives to light bundles of aromatic juniper boughs in the ovens made for the purpose on the roofs of their homes, and as the fragrant smoke ascends to heaven they sing a hymn or litany in which the men of the house often join, the deep voices of the latter and the clear high notes of the former blending most agreeably with the distant music in the lamaseries; in the morning juniper boughs are again burnt, with offerings - bowls of water, wine, milk, or butter lamps - placed before the household gods.
summary.zh: 藏人家最動人者，莫過暮禱：夜幕垂落，寺中佛壇燃燈，僧眾誦短經，廊下喇嘛以長銅號與單簧管奏哀婉之曲——這是主婦們的號令：於屋頂專設的爐中點燃香柏枝，青煙裊裊上達於天，婦女們唱起讚美詩或連禱文，男子亦常隨聲相和，低沉男聲與清亮女聲，與遠處寺院的樂音交融無間。晨間復焚柏枝，以水、酒、乳、酥油燈供於家神之前。

sensitivity.note: Living household devotion; paraphrase of public-domain travel record.

passages.text: It is a universal custom among this people, before eating or drinking anything, to dip the forefinger of the right hand in it and scatter a little of the contents towards the four cardinal points, reciting a short prayer the while; this and the mumbling of the mani prayer are practically the only religious observances of the people. And they have another way of showing their religious feelings, that love of mankind dear to Buddhism - this is, in multiplying for the weal of sentient creation written or sculptured copies of the mani prayer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rockhill, The Land of the Lamas (1891); not verbatim.
